events/nine-saints-ethiopia-480/title: Arrival of the Nine Saints in Ethiopia
events/nine-saints-ethiopia-480/summary: Ethiopian tradition tells of nine monks from the Roman East, probably non-Chalcedonians, who came to Aksum in the late fifth century, founded monasteries such as Debre Damo, evangelised the countryside and translated Scripture and texts into Ge'ez. They gave Ethiopian Christianity its monastic and Miaphysite character.
events/nine-saints-ethiopia-480/causes/0: Flight of anti-Chalcedonian monks from imperial pressure
events/school-of-nisibis-489/title: School of the Persians moves to Nisibis
events/school-of-nisibis-489/summary: Emperor Zeno closed the 'School of the Persians' at Edessa for its Antiochene (Dyophysite) theology; its teachers, led by Narsai, reestablished it at Nisibis under Bishop Barsauma in Persian territory. Nisibis became the theological academy of the Church of the East, which at synods in 484–486 formally adopted Theodore of Mopsuestia's theology.
events/school-of-nisibis-489/consequence: Intellectual centre for the Church of the East for two centuries
Transmission of Greek learning into Syriac and later Arabic
events/baptism-of-clovis-496/title: Baptism of Clovis, king of the Franks
events/baptism-of-clovis-496/summary: Clovis, influenced by his Catholic wife Clotilde and a victory over the Alamanni, was baptized by Bishop Remigius at Reims (dates range 496–508). Unlike other Germanic kings, who were Homoian, he chose Nicene Catholicism, aligning the Franks with the Gallo-Roman bishops and the papacy.
events/baptism-of-clovis-496/consequence: Foundation of the later Carolingian alliance with Rome
events/benedict-at-monte-cassino-529/sum: Benedict of Nursia established a monastery on Monte Cassino and wrote his Rule, a moderate guide to communal prayer, work and obedience drawing on earlier masters. Through Carolingian promotion it became the standard rule of Western monasticism.
events/benedict-at-monte-cassino-529/cau: Desire for ordered communal life amid social collapse
events/benedict-at-monte-cassino-529/con: Preservation of learning and liturgy in the West
events/council-of-orange-529/summary: A small Gallic council under Caesarius of Arles condemned 'Semi-Pelagian' views that the beginning of faith lies in human free will, affirming that even the first movement toward God is a gift of grace. It did not endorse double predestination, which it explicitly rejected. Pope Boniface II confirmed it in 531.
events/council-of-orange-529/causes/0: Debates following Augustine's death, involving John Cassian and Faustus of Riez
events/council-of-orange-529/consequence: Rediscovered in the 16th century and cited by Catholics and Protestants alike
events/hagia-sophia-dedicated-537/summar: Justinian rebuilt the Great Church of Holy Wisdom with a vast dome by Anthemius and Isidore, dedicated on 27 December 537. It became the symbol of Byzantine Orthodoxy; the Russian Primary Chronicle credits its liturgy with persuading Vladimir's envoys.
events/hagia-sophia-dedicated-537/causes: Nika riots destroyed the previous church (532)
events/jacob-baradaeus-ordinations-542/t: Jacob Baradaeus builds a Miaphysite hierarchy
events/jacob-baradaeus-ordinations-542/s: Consecrated secretly bishop of Edessa with the help of Empress Theodora, Jacob Baradaeus travelled in disguise across Syria and Asia Minor ordaining bishops and priests. He gave the anti-Chalcedonian church of Syria an independent hierarchy; its members were long called 'Jacobites'.
events/jacob-baradaeus-ordinations-542/c: Syriac Orthodox Church as a separate communion
events/conversion-of-nubia-543/summary: Rival missions sent by Theodora (Miaphysite) and Justinian (Chalcedonian) reached the Nubian kingdoms of Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia between 543 and 580. Christian Nubia flourished for some 800 years, with cathedrals such as Faras decorated with remarkable frescoes.
events/second-council-of-constantinople-: Justinian, hoping to reconcile the Miaphysites, had the council condemn the 'Three Chapters' — writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret and Ibas — and interpret Chalcedon in a Cyrilline sense. Pope Vigilius, held in Constantinople, resisted and then acquiesced; the council also condemned Origenist teachings.

The Fifth Ecumenical Council is the clearest case of an emperor driving doctrine. Justinian believed that if Chalcedon was shown to be fully compatible with Cyril, and if the Antiochene theologians most offensive to Miaphysites were condemned, the anti-Chalcedonian majority in Egypt and Syria could be won back. The council's canons stress that the Word 'one of the Trinity' suffered in the flesh (theopaschism) and that the union is 'hypostatic'. Pope Vigilius, who had been brought to the capital, first refused, then submitted; churches in northern Italy and Africa broke communion with Rome for decades (the Schism of the Three Chapters). The Miaphysites were not reconciled, and the Church of the East, which revered Theodore as 'the Interpreter', was further estranged. Orthodox and Catholic churches count the council as ecumenical; Protestants vary in their regard for councils after Chalcedon.
Justinian's search for unity with Miaphysites
events/columba-founds-iona-563/summary: The Irish monk Columba (Colum Cille) sailed with twelve companions to Iona, founding a monastery that evangelised the Picts of Scotland and, through Aidan of Lindisfarne (635), much of northern England.
events/columba-founds-iona-563/consequen: Celtic Christianity in Scotland and Northumbria
events/second-council-of-macon-585/title: Second Council of Mâcon orders the tithe
events/second-council-of-macon-585/summa: A Frankish council at Mâcon commands the faithful to pay tithes under pain of excommunication, an early step toward the compulsory ecclesiastical tithe that Charlemagne’s capitularies (779) made law across his empire.
events/second-council-of-macon-585/conse: Later anticlerical tithe revolts and abolitions (France 1789)
events/council-of-toledo-589/summary: King Reccared and the Visigothic nobility renounced Homoian ('Arian') Christianity for Catholic Nicene faith. The council's creed included the Holy Spirit's procession from the Father 'and the Son' (Filioque), an early step toward the later East–West dispute.
events/council-of-toledo-589/causes/1: Desire to unify Goths and Hispano-Romans
events/council-of-toledo-589/consequence: Spread of the Filioque in Western creeds
events/mission-to-england-597/title: Gregory the Great's mission to the English
events/mission-to-england-597/summary: Pope Gregory I sent Augustine, prior of his Roman monastery, with about forty monks to Kent, where King Æthelberht, whose wife Bertha was Christian, was baptized. Gregory's letters advised adapting pagan temples and festivals rather than destroying them.
events/mission-to-england-597/consequenc: Roman-oriented English church, later meeting Celtic missions
events/rise-of-islam-arab-conquests-634/: Rise of Islam and the Arab conquests

After Muhammad's death (632), Arab armies conquered Byzantine Syria, Palestine and Egypt and the Sasanian Empire within two decades, then North Africa and Spain by 711. Most Christians of the Middle East — Chalcedonian, Miaphysite and Church of the East — became protected but subordinate dhimmi communities under Muslim rule.

The conquests were the decisive geopolitical event of Christian late antiquity. Jerusalem surrendered to Caliph Umar in 638, Alexandria in 641–642, Ctesiphon fell in 637. For many non-Chalcedonian Christians, Arab rule at first meant relief from Byzantine pressure; Christians served as administrators, physicians and translators, and the Church of the East reached its greatest extent under the Abbasids. Over centuries, however, the jizya tax, legal disabilities, periodic persecution and social incentives led to gradual conversion, Arabisation and decline, so that Christians became minorities in lands that had been Christian heartlands. The loss of Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem to Muslim rule left Rome and Constantinople as the chief Christian centres and shifted Christianity's centre of gravity northward and westward. Islam's critique of the Trinity and of images also shaped Christian theology, from John of Damascus to the iconoclast debates.
Exhaustion of Rome and Persia after the war of 602–628
Patriarchates of Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem under Muslim rule
Long-term decline of Christianity in the Middle East and North Africa
events/alopen-reaches-chang-an-635/title: Alopen brings the 'Luminous Religion' to China
events/alopen-reaches-chang-an-635/summa: A Church of the East mission led by Alopen arrived at the Tang capital Chang'an, where Emperor Taizong received him, had the scriptures translated and in 638 authorised a monastery. The Xi'an Stele of 781 recounts the mission and summarises the faith in Chinese, Buddhist and Daoist vocabulary.
events/alopen-reaches-chang-an-635/cause: Church of the East networks along the Silk Road
events/synod-of-whitby-664/summary: King Oswiu of Northumbria, hosted by Abbess Hilda, heard the Irish party (Colman) and the Roman party (Wilfrid) argue over the date of Easter and the tonsure. Oswiu chose Roman usage, citing Peter's keys, which drew the English church into closer conformity with Rome.
events/synod-of-whitby-664/causes/0: Different Easter calculations in one royal household
events/synod-of-whitby-664/consequences/: Withdrawal of Irish monks from Lindisfarne
events/third-council-of-constantinople-6: The Sixth Ecumenical Council condemned Monothelitism, the imperial compromise teaching one will in Christ, and affirmed two natural wills and operations, divine and human, in harmony. It vindicated Maximus the Confessor, mutilated and exiled for his opposition, and condemned Pope Honorius I posthumously.

Monoenergism and Monothelitism were launched by Patriarch Sergius and Emperor Heraclius in the 620s–630s to win back the Miaphysites as the empire fought Persia and then the Arabs. Maximus the Confessor argued that a nature without its own will would be incomplete, and that Christ's human will, freely obedient to the divine, is the place where human freedom is healed; with Pope Martin I he secured condemnation of Monothelitism at the Lateran Synod of 649, for which both suffered. The council of 680–681 under Constantine IV affirmed 'two natural wills and two natural operations, without division, change, separation or confusion'. Its anathema on Honorius was later cited in debates over papal infallibility at Vatican I. Maronite tradition maintains that its church was never Monothelite, a point historians debate.
Honorius question in later papal debates
events/council-in-trullo-692/summary: Council held in the domed hall (trullos) of the imperial palace in Constantinople under Justinian II; its canons, accepted by the Orthodox but not by Rome, permit priests and deacons married before ordination to keep their wives (canon 13, criticising Roman practice) while requiring bishops to be celibate (canon 48).
events/council-in-trullo-692/consequence: Enduring Eastern discipline of married parish clergy and celibate bishops
